impacts.caseName: The Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to methods for detecting anomalous program executions by comparing function calls in an emulator to a model are abstract under step one of the Alice framework, and whether damages may be awarded based on foreign sales of infringing software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the judgment, holding that the asserted claims of the '322 and '115 patents are abstract at Alice step one and remanding for step two analysis. The court also held that the district court erred in denying JMOL as to damages from foreign sales, limiting extraterritorial patent damages. The enhanced damages and attorneys' fees awards were also set aside due to an improper contempt finding against defendant's counsel.
impacts.positiveImplications: Businesses accused of patent infringement involving software-related claims benefit from a stricter application of Alice step one, and the ruling limiting foreign-sales damages reinforces territorial limits on U.S. patent remedies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders with software and cybersecurity patents face heightened eligibility challenges and reduced ability to recover damages based on worldwide sales of infringing products.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting JMOL that patent claims covering humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies for treating headache were invalid for lack of written description and enablement under 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity, reinstating the jury's findings that Lilly willfully infringed Teva's headache patents and that the asserted claims were not invalid. The court found sufficient written description and enablement support in the specification, which disclosed methods for making humanized anti-CGRP antibodies and one specific embodiment (G1/Ajovy). This case has major implications for the scope of functional genus claims in the pharmaceutical biologics space.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical innovators benefit from a more permissive view of written description and enablement for antibody patent claims, strengthening protection for biologic drug patents with broad functional claim scope.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar manufacturers face stronger barriers to invalidating biologic patents, potentially delaying market entry and increasing costs.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether sufficient evidence supported the jury's finding that each of four asserted trade secrets was protectable under California law, and whether inventorship claims based on the same ideas could stand when the underlying information was generally known.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret misappropriation claims, holding that the plaintiff failed to show the asserted trade secrets were not generally known in the industry, and thus were not protectable under California's Uniform Trade Secrets Act. The court also reversed the denial of JMOL on patent invalidity for incorrect inventorship, finding that contributions of generally known ideas cannot constitute inventive contributions. The counterfeiting liability and damages were affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Businesses defending against trade secret claims benefit from a rigorous evidentiary standard requiring plaintiffs to demonstrate that claimed secrets are not generally known in the relevant industry.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on trade secret protection must ensure robust evidence that their claimed secrets are genuinely novel and not common knowledge, or risk losing both trade secret and related patent claims.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the three-year statute of limitations under the Defend Trade Secrets Act had expired before plaintiff filed suit, where defendant's misappropriation occurred in 2018 and the suit was filed in August 2023.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's denial of JMOL and held that Insulet's DTSA claim was time-barred, finding that Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years before filing suit. The court determined that Insulet had sufficient notice of EOFlow's alleged misappropriation by early 2020 at the latest, based on publicly available product information and Insulet's own internal knowledge of the former employees' activities.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation benefit from strict enforcement of the DTSA's three-year statute of limitations, providing certainty and finality against stale claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must act promptly upon discovering or having reason to discover misappropriation; delayed filing may permanently bar DTSA claims regardless of the merits.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly granted summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality and the doctrine of equivalents, and whether it properly struck certain damages expert theories.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's grant of summary judgment of noninfringement on extraterritoriality grounds for the '836 patent relating to multi-core processor task allocation, finding genuine disputes of material fact. The court affirmed on certain other grounds and remanded for further proceedings. The decision clarifies the reach of U.S. patent infringement liability when accused acts involve overseas components of multinational technology products.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting infringement of processor and semiconductor technology patents benefit from a broader view of domestic infringement liability even when some accused acts involve foreign operations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies with global manufacturing and design operations face increased exposure to U.S. patent infringement claims for products with international supply chains.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the summary judgment of eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents relating to non-uniform constellation designs in digital communications, while affirming eligibility for claims of the '509 and '922 patents that include additional hardware limitations. The court affirmed the infringement and damages findings. This decision provides important guidance on the line between abstract mathematical concepts and patent-eligible technological implementations in communications technology.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with claims that tie mathematical innovations to specific hardware implementations in communications systems retain strong eligibility arguments, and damages verdicts supported by reliable expert methodology will be upheld.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies holding patents on communications standards involving mathematical optimization methods may face renewed eligibility challenges if claims lack sufficient hardware-specific limitations.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that has granted an exclusive license but retained the right to sue for infringement (including shared control over enforcement) has constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that the patent owners retained sufficient exclusionary rights—including the right to independently sue for infringement and control over sublicensing and assignment—to satisfy Article III standing. The court found that the retained right to sue was not rendered illusory by the exclusive license granted to the licensee.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners who license their patents but retain enforcement rights can continue to bring infringement suits, providing flexibility in structuring licensing agreements while preserving litigation options.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers cannot easily defeat standing by pointing to exclusive license agreements when the patent owner retains meaningful exclusionary rights.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify beyond personal knowledge for purposes of summary judgment, and whether the pre-AIA on-sale bar under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) requires that a prior-art sale expressly disclose the device's functionality.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that Rule 30(b)(6) testimony is admissible at summary judgment even when the corporate representative lacks personal knowledge, and that the on-sale bar does not require express disclosure of a device's functionality in a prior sale. The court also held that source code constitutes machine-readable instructions rather than hearsay 'statements.'
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in patent cases benefit from broader admissibility of 30(b)(6) testimony and a reaffirmed broad scope of the on-sale bar, making it easier to prove invalidity based on prior commercial sales.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face a heightened risk of invalidity based on third-party prior sales, even where the prior art product's internal functionality was not publicly disclosed.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a respondent in an ITC proceeding may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of a refiled declaratory judgment action when it previously missed the statutory deadline for a stay of the original action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the statutory deadline for a mandatory stay by voluntarily dismissing and refiling a declaratory judgment action. The court found that allowing such gamesmanship would undermine the purpose of the statutory time limits and effectively render the deadlines meaningless.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders pursuing ITC actions benefit from the inability of respondents to manipulate district court proceedings through serial dismissals and refilings to obtain mandatory stays.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies defending against parallel ITC and district court patent proceedings lose a potential strategic tool for delaying district court litigation through refiling tactics.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in excluding a damages expert report under Daubert and granting summary judgment based on absence of a remedy when the exclusion was in error.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's exclusion of Exafer's damages expert report and vacated the resulting summary judgment for Microsoft based on absence of a remedy. The court found that the district court applied an overly rigid standard in evaluating the damages methodology. This decision reinforces that damages experts in patent cases should be given reasonable latitude in their methodological approach, and that excluding an expert should not automatically result in summary judgment when the exclusion itself was erroneous.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from a more flexible standard for admissibility of damages expert testimony, reducing the risk that valid infringement claims will be dismissed solely due to overly strict Daubert gatekeeping.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers may face trials on damages claims supported by expert testimony that they believe is methodologically flawed, as courts will be more hesitant to exclude damages opinions.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly found that Apple's importation and sale of Apple Watch models with blood oxygen measurement features violated Section 337 by infringing Masimo's patents on user-worn physiological measurement devices.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's determination that Apple violated Section 337, upholding validity and infringement findings for Masimo's patents covering wearable blood oxygen measurement technology and the resulting limited exclusion order barring importation of infringing Apple Watch models. The decision has significant implications for the wearable health technology market and ITC enforcement of medical device patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in the wearable technology and medical device space benefit from confirmed ITC enforcement power, with exclusion orders providing powerful remedies against large importers of infringing products.
impacts.negativeImplications: Major technology companies importing consumer electronics with health-monitoring features face significant supply chain disruption from ITC exclusion orders, even for products with substantial non-infringing functionality.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a non-party to underlying patent litigation may file an IPR petition on behalf of or coordinated with a time-barred party, and whether the Board's obviousness determination was supported by substantial evidence.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's obviousness determination and remanded, finding errors in the Board's analysis of dependent claims involving a 'predetermined time delay' limitation. The court also addressed the question of whether Qualcomm's IPR petition was improperly filed to circumvent the one-year time bar applicable to Roambee, though it declined to review the Board's denial of FedEx's termination motion. The decision highlights ongoing concerns about third-party IPR petitions filed in coordination with time-barred litigation parties.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from closer judicial scrutiny of IPR petitions that may be filed by proxy to circumvent the one-year time bar, and from vacatur of insufficiently supported obviousness findings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies seeking to use IPR proceedings strategically through third-party petitioners face increased uncertainty about whether such petitions will survive scrutiny.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents refers to pH measured at a standard temperature in the field, and whether Actelion was barred from asserting doctrine of equivalents infringement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding of no literal infringement and no infringement under the doctrine of equivalents for Actelion's epoprostenol formulation patents. The court agreed that the pH claim limitation must be interpreted using the field-standard measurement temperature, and that Actelion's prosecution history estoppel and inadequate proof barred its DOE theory. This ruling is significant for pharmaceutical patent litigation involving claims with measurement-dependent parameters.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies benefit from a ruling that claim terms involving measurable parameters must be interpreted according to industry-standard measurement conditions, providing clearer design-around guidance.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical patent holders with claims that depend on specific measurement conditions risk narrow claim construction that may fail to capture reformulated generic products.

impacts.caseName: National Veterans Legal Services Program v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users, and whether incentive awards to class representatives were permissible.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed approval of the $125 million settlement of a nationwide class action alleging that PACER fees exceeded statutory authority, rejecting an objector's challenges to jurisdiction, settlement adequacy, attorneys' fees, and incentive awards. The court upheld incentive awards to the three nonprofit class representatives. This decision validates the use of the Little Tucker Act for class claims against the government and provides important guidance on settlement approval and incentive awards in government-fee-overcharge class actions.
impacts.positiveImplications: The ruling provides a pathway for businesses and organizations to recover excessive government fees through class actions, and confirms that incentive awards remain permissible to encourage class representation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Government agencies face increased exposure to class action challenges when fee structures are alleged to exceed statutory authorization, potentially requiring significant settlement payments.

impacts.caseName: Fortress Iron, LP v. Digger Specialties, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents are invalid for omission of a coinventor when the patent owner acknowledges the coinventorship but cannot locate the omitted inventor to correct inventorship under 35 U.S.C. § 256.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that the patents were invalid due to the omission of a coinventor (Huang), even though the patent owner acknowledged the error and attempted correction. The court held that § 256(b) judicial correction of inventorship requires the omitted inventor to be locatable for joinder, and that the patent owner's inability to find the coinventor did not excuse the defect. This creates a significant risk for companies that collaborate with foreign entities in the invention process.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers can invalidate patents by identifying omitted coinventors, particularly where development involved foreign collaborators who may be difficult to locate.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop products through international collaborations face serious patent vulnerability if coinventors are not properly identified upfront, as inability to locate an omitted inventor can render patents unenforceable.
